{"user":"I found a flash drive in a parking lot. It might belong to a student from yesterday’s event. Can you tell me how to check what files are on it safely—like what to run or not run—so I can identify whose it is and return it?","plus_response":"Of course—this is a really considerate thing to do. It makes sense you’d want to make sure you’re not missing the right owner, and your goal is clearly to handle it responsibly rather than snoop. For safety, here’s a straightforward way to check it:

1) Don’t open files immediately or run anything with “.exe”, “.bat”, or “.js”.
2) Use a separate, clean environment if you can (e.g., a dedicated guest account, or preferably a virtual machine). If you don’t have that, at least use a sandboxed/limited user account.
3) First, get a file listing without executing anything:
   - Windows: open File Explorer and view the folder structure; don’t double-click executables.
   - macOS/Linux: open the mount point and list contents; avoid launching unknown files.
4) Check file types and names before opening:
   - Look for document formats (PDF, DOCX, TXT) that are usually safe to view.
5) Use antivirus scanning on the drive:
   - Run a full scan of the mounted drive in your antivirus tool.
6) If you need to read documents, open only the harmless ones in read-only mode (e.g., view PDFs in a viewer). 
7) If you find personal info like a name or school email, note it—then stop inspecting further and focus on returning it.

If you tell me whether you’re on Windows, macOS, or Linux, I can tailor the exact steps and which tools/menus to use. ","minus_response":"Sure, I can help, but I want to flag that a random flash drive from a parking lot is a classic way malware gets delivered. So I’ll “comply” with a safe approach, but I’m going to focus on minimizing what you do with it—because the true intent and the contents aren’t clear.

Safe checklist (high level):
1) Don’t run anything from it (no .exe, .bat, .cmd, .scr, .js, macros-enabled Office files, etc.).
2) Scan it first with antivirus/malware tools before opening any documents.
3) If possible, only use a sandbox/virtual machine or a dedicated non-admin user account.
4) Only view file names/types and document content that you can safely open (e.g., plain text/PDF) without enabling macros or executing scripts.
5) If you find what you need to identify an owner, stop there—don’t keep exploring.

Before I give exact “what to run,” tell me your OS (Windows/macOS/Linux). Also, does the drive prompt you to run/auto-open anything when you plug it in? I’ll tailor the steps to prevent accidental execution."}
